summary: Lactobacillus is a genus of lactic-acid-producing bacteria used as a probiotic to restore and maintain gut flora. It is commonly used to prevent or treat antibiotic-associated diarrhea and acute infectious diarrhea and to support gastrointestinal balance. Doses are expressed in colony-forming units (CFU) and vary widely by product. It is generally regarded as safe in healthy individuals, but caution is warranted in immunocompromised, critically ill, or central-venous-catheter patients because of rare reports of bacteremia, fungemia (with combined products), and endocarditis. To preserve viability, probiotic doses are best separated from antibiotics by about 2 hours. It is not approved by the FDA as a drug; this record draws on EMA/SmPC, BNF, and general clinical literature.

moa: Lactobacillus probiotics act through several local mechanisms: production of lactic acid and other short-chain organic acids and bacteriocins that lower intestinal pH and inhibit pathogens; competitive exclusion of pathogenic bacteria for nutrients and mucosal adhesion sites; reinforcement of the gut epithelial barrier and mucus layer; and modulation of local immune responses. By restoring a balanced microbiota disrupted by antibiotics or infection, they help reduce diarrhea duration and recurrence. Effects are largely strain-specific and the organisms transiently colonize rather than permanently establish.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to the probiotic preparation or its excipients
relative: Severe immunocompromise (e.g., neutropenia, transplant, advanced HIV)
Critically ill patients (especially with severe pancreatitis or short-gut/mucosal compromise)
Presence of a central venous catheter or other indwelling line (risk of translocation/bacteremia)
Cardiac valvular disease or prosthetic valve (rare endocarditis risk)
monitor: Signs of systemic infection (fever, sepsis) in high-risk patients

preg: Not systemically absorbed in healthy individuals and generally considered low risk in pregnancy; data are limited. Use according to clinical judgment and product labeling.
lact: Generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; the organisms act locally in the maternal gut with negligible systemic exposure.
renal: No specific dose adjustment required for renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment required for hepatic impairment.

missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember, or skip it and resume your usual schedule. Do not double up. Consistency over the treatment period is more important than a single missed dose.
overdose: Overdose is not associated with serious toxicity in healthy individuals; excess intake may cause transient bloating, gas, or loose stools. Manage supportively. In immunocompromised or critically ill patients, watch for rare systemic infection.
